name: Outbound — the outside-processing control tower for machine shops
one_liner: For the buyer/quality manager at a 10-80 person precision machine shop, Outbound owns the parts that leave the building: it builds each heat-treat/plating/anodize vendor PO with the exact spec revision and quality clauses flowed down from the customer PO, chases the processor by email for a promised date, and checks the returned certificate against what was required before the job is released to ship.
problem: A precision machine shop finishes machining and then sends the lot out to a heat treater, anodizer or plater. From that moment the job disappears from the shop's control: the ERP shows a planned operation and a vendor PO, but nobody knows the real return date until someone phones the processor. Two concrete failures recur. (1) Date blindness: shops add a blanket buffer (a scheduling write-up describes a shop using a flat five-day buffer and still missing about a quarter of its jobs — illustrative, not a survey) and only discover the slip when the customer ship date is days away. (2) Paperwork failure: the customer PO invokes a quality clause (spec + revision, Nadcap-approved source, cert content, traceability, right of access). Someone has to copy that into the processor PO by hand, then check the cert that comes back. Get the revision wrong or lose the cert and the consequence is a shipment hold, a SCAR, an audit finding, reprocessing or a scrapped lot; one published aerospace supplier term sheet charges $250 per shipment for missing certifications (pccairfoils.com), and lot traceability that can't be substantiated can mean scrap. Today the workaround is a buyer or quality clerk with a spreadsheet, a whiteboard, a reminder calendar and a phone. Perplexity's review of JobBOSS², ProShop and Fulcrum found no evidence any of them natively emails processors for status or auto-files returned certs against the PO requirement — the automation examples that exist (WebRun on JobBOSS, netray on ProShop) are third-party bolt-ons that only draft follow-up emails.
target_customer: Owner / general manager, or the buyer-scheduler, at a US precision machine shop of 10-80 people that does aerospace, defense or medical work and sends 20-200 lots a month to outside processors. Buyer is the owner (they sign the $200-800/month software decisions) or the quality manager who owns AS9100 8.4.3 flowdown. US Census-derived counts put roughly 16,300 machine-shop establishments under 50 employees (NAICS 332710); the AS9100/defense-exposed slice is the beachhead.
why_now: Three things changed. (1) Document AI finally reads the messy inputs: a customer PO PDF with clause IDs, a 40-page supplier quality manual, a scanned plating cert. a16z's 2026 Big Idea "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li, https://a16z.com/newsletter/big-ideas-2026-part-1/) names exactly this bottleneck, and LandingAI already markets CoC-vs-PO/BOM checking for electronics receiving — proof the technique works, just not for this buyer. (2) Email/voice agents that chase suppliers for promised dates became a product category in 2026 — HappyRobot's manufacturers-and-suppliers offering, Conversight Supply Assurance, VoiceRun — but all three are enterprise-shaped; HappyRobot's own materials say it targets ~$1B+ revenue companies and is not for small-business self-serve. The capability exists; nobody has packaged it for a 25-person shop. (3) Demand pressure: PwC reports a commercial aircraft backlog near 15,000 units and a defense backlog up more than 50% in three years; an Oliver Wyman survey reported 45% of suppliers saying they could not double output within a year. Shops are taking on more aerospace/defense work, and that work is the kind that comes with clause flowdown and cert packages. Also relevant: YC's latest RFS "The $15-an-Hour Expert" (Brad Flora, https://www.ycombinator.com/rfs#the-15-an-hour-expert) — this is literally letting a shop's shipping clerk do the quality manager's flowdown review.
comparables: ProShop ERP (proshoperp.com) — job shop ERP, tracks out-of-plant parts and vendor POs as routing steps; estimated ~$500-715/mo small-shop. Gap: it records what was requested, not what the processor is doing now; no evidence of automated vendor chasing or cert-to-requirement matching. JobBOSS² (erpresearch.com/erp/jobboss) — outside-processing POs with cost roll-up; the only "flag overdue and draft follow-up email" capability found is a third-party automation layer (webrun.ai/automate/apps/jobboss), which is evidence the hole exists. Fulcrum — cloud ERP/MES; reviews surface accounting and date-entry complaints, nothing confirming this workflow. GroundControl (gndctl.com, YC, ~$3M seed) — closest adjacent: aerospace PO review (customer PO vs quote, clause extraction) plus FAI review, priced per facility. Gap: it reviews the incoming customer PO; it does not, per its public material, generate the outgoing processor PO, chase the processor, or match the returned cert to the invoked spec revision. This is the most likely future competitor and also the strongest proof the problem is real and fundable. 1factory (1factory.com, $75/user/mo) — CoC management, NCR/CAPA/SCAR; a records system, not an agent that chases. HappyRobot / Conversight Supply Assurance / VoiceRun — AI agents that call suppliers for revised PO dates; enterprise-priced and enterprise-scoped, explicitly not SMB self-serve. LandingAI — checks incoming CoCs against PO/BOM specs, but sold to electronics/industrial enterprises, not job shops. Lantek Integra Outsourcing — external work orders with linked certs, but only inside the Lantek suite. Net gap: nobody sells a standalone, ERP-agnostic tool to a 25-person shop that covers the full loop — flow the clause down, chase the date, verify the cert.
market_note: Estimate, stated as such. ~16,300 US machine-shop establishments under 50 employees (Census/BLS-derived, NAICS 332710), plus larger shops and fabricators. Assume 15-20% do enough regulated outside processing to care: ~2,500-3,500 beachhead accounts in the US alone. At $400/month that is a ~$12-17M ARR beachhead before expanding to medical device CMs, fabricators and the finishing shops on the other side of the transaction. Willingness to pay is anchored by what these shops already pay: Uptool publishes $195/month with most shops at $195-495 (uptool.com/pricing); 1factory lists Quality Control at $75/user/month with a 5-user minimum (~$375/month floor) including CoC management and SCAR workflows; ProShop is estimated by third parties around $500-715/month for small shops. So $300-600/month sits inside an established budget band. The honest caveat: no public data proves a shop will add a line item specifically for outside processing, and no reliable benchmark exists for days lost at processors or the share of late jobs they cause — that is the thing to validate.
risks: 1) ERP gravity: shops may insist this belongs in ProShop/JobBOSS, and one of those incumbents (or GroundControl, which already owns the customer-PO side and has YC money) can ship the chase-and-verify loop as a feature. The defence is being ERP-agnostic and email-native so a shop with no ERP can use it. 2) The pain may be owned by nobody: in a 25-person shop the buyer, the quality manager and the owner each touch a piece, so the tool can fall between chairs and never get a champion or a budget line. 3) Reliability of the cert check: a false "cert OK" on an aerospace lot is worse than no tool. The product must position as a reviewer that flags and blocks, never as an auto-approver, which caps how much labour it removes early on. 4) Distribution is slow and physical — trade shows, Practical Machinist, referrals — which is far from this builder's X-native launch style.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) That date-chasing plus cert-verification together are worth a separate line item, rather than being tolerated as "part of the buyer's job." Evidence for the pain is strong; evidence for standalone willingness to pay is not — no vendor was found selling exactly this, which is both the gap and the warning. 2) That a shop will forward its customer POs, supplier quality manuals and processor certs to a cloud tool. ITAR/CUI-exposed shops may refuse — Uptool prices ITAR separately and GroundControl pursued FedRAMP-moderate equivalency, which says this objection is real and costly. 3) That clause flowdown can be extracted reliably enough from heterogeneous customer quality manuals (every prime has its own clause document and revision) that the generated processor PO is trustworthy on the first pass.
first_customers: Ten 15-60 person AS9100-certified machine shops in a single metro cluster (Wichita, Phoenix, Connecticut river valley, Orange County CA) that already ship aerospace or defense parts and use three or more outside processors. Find them via: the Nadcap/eAuditNet and AS9100 certification directories cross-referenced with Google Maps "CNC machining" in those metros; finishing.com's shop directory read in reverse (ask anodizers and heat treaters which machine shops chase them most); Practical Machinist and r/Machinists threads on late outside processing; and the exhibitor list of a regional show (Westec/IMTS). Warm path: approach the processors first — they are drowning in status phone calls and will happily introduce their worst-chasing customers.
validation_test: This week, email or call 15 AS9100 shops with one ask: "Send me last month's outside-processing POs and the cert PDFs that came back — I'll return a one-page report showing which lots came back late versus the promised date, and which certs are missing a required spec revision or clause." Do it by hand with an LLM; no product. Pass if 5 of 15 send real files AND at least 3 of those reports surface a genuine miss (a late lot nobody tracked, or a cert that does not match the invoked revision), AND 2 of them say yes to a $300/month paid pilot for the same report running weekly. Fail if shops say "our buyer already has that in a spreadsheet and it's fine" — that kills the budget-line assumption and the idea should go back to the shelf.
build_plan: Narrowest sellable version: an email-native outside-processing tracker, no ERP integration. 1) Shop forwards (or BCCs) its processor POs to a dedicated address; an agent parses part number, lot, process, spec+revision, qty and due date into a board of "parts currently out." 2) Flowdown builder: upload the customer PO plus the prime's quality-clause document once; the agent extracts the invoked clauses for that part and generates the processor PO text (spec + revision, required cert contents, traceability, approved-source note) as a copy-paste block or PDF — human approves before sending, always. 3) Chase agent: on a schedule, emails the processor ("status and promised return date for PO 4412?"), parses the reply, updates the promised date, and raises one daily digest of at-risk lots to the buyer. 4) Cert check: when the processor emails the cert back, the agent matches it to the lot and checks it against the requirements captured in step 2 — spec, revision, lot ID, signature, test values present — and marks the job green/amber/red before shipping. 5) Ship-ready view: one screen per customer PO showing every outside op and its cert status. Cut for v1: voice calling, ERP write-back, scheduling/capacity, FAI/ballooning, mobile apps, supplier portals, multi-tier flowdown. Stack fits the builder: TypeScript, an inbound email service, a document model API, a simple hosted app; the agent orchestration is exactly UiPath/Maestro-shaped work. Sell it as a $300-600/month service with the first month run manually behind the scenes.
launch_post: Parts go out to heat treat and vanish. We built an agent that emails the processor for a real return date, and checks the cert that comes back against the spec revision your customer actually invoked — before you ship. For machine shops. No ERP required.
reasoning: Outbound won because it is the boring step next to a hot category. Two bookmarks pointed at American manufacturing (twentyfour26's autonomous CNC factory) and at agents doing real work; every obvious manufacturing idea — instant quoting, DFM, FAI reports — turned out to be fully occupied by funded players within one screening call. The step nobody had taken was the one where the shop loses control: the parts that leave the building. Research confirmed three things that matter. First, the obligation is real and specific: AS9100 8.4.3 requires the shop to flow the customer's invoked spec, revision and approved-source requirements down to the heat treater or plater, and the failures (wrong revision, missing cert, non-approved source) produce SCARs, shipment holds and scrapped lots — one published supplier term sheet even charges $250 per shipment for missing certs. Second, the gap is confirmed by incumbents' own shape: ProShop, JobBOSS² and Fulcrum record the outside-process PO but there is no evidence any of them chases the processor or matches a returned cert to the invoked requirement; the only such automations found are third-party bolt-ons written for those ERPs, which is people paying to patch a hole. Third, the 2026 agents that do chase suppliers — HappyRobot, Conversight, VoiceRun — are explicitly enterprise; HappyRobot's own material says it is not for small-business self-serve. That leaves 16,300-odd sub-50-employee US machine shops with the obligation, the consequence and no product. GroundControl (YC, ~$3M seed) is the nearest threat and validates the category, but it reviews the incoming customer PO; Outbound owns the outgoing processor PO and the cert that comes back. It differs from the filed Shortfall and Dockproof ideas in buyer and workflow: Shortfall reconciles insurance commissions, Dockproof prevents retail chargebacks pre-ship for CPG brands; Outbound governs a regulated subcontract operation and its document package for a machine shop. Fit for this builder is good — email-in agents, document parsing and approval workflows are exactly UiPath/Maestro-shaped — but this is a 3+ month venture with a trade-show-and-referral sales motion, not an X-native launch, and the builder should go in knowing that. It is 7.8 and not higher because one thing is genuinely unproven: no public data shows a small shop will add a separate line item for this, and I found no benchmark for days lost at outside processors. That single unknown is what the week-one validation test is built to hit.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Outbound — outside-processing control tower for machine shops (flowdown + chase + cert verify). PICK. Named buyer, recurring weekly pain with real financial consequence, confirmed gap in every ERP checked, price band already established by Uptool/1factory.
2. Sipse-style friction-free investing for Indian retail (from @misbahspeaks). Dropped at generation — consumer fintech, heavily regulated, not B2B, no agent edge for this builder.
3. MFD commission reconciliation for Indian mutual fund distributors (adjacent to the Sipse bookmark). Dropped at screen — Mindstack, Creso, REDVision and others already ship AMC payout ingestion and trail reconciliation for MFDs; also near-identical in shape to the filed idea Shortfall (carrier commission reconciliation), so a repeat.
4. Dependency cooldown / minimum-release-age policy enforcement with approvals (from the Jack Cable security bookmark). Dropped at screen — Safeguard.sh already sells configurable package-age policies, gates and exception approval across npm and PyPI; Socket and Aikido are moving in; and it is a developer-tools idea in a crowded market, which this library already has plenty of.
5. Instant-quote / DFM precheck for CNC job shops (from the twentyfour26 bookmark). Dropped at screen — Paperless Parts, Uptool ($195/mo), AMFG, CloudNC Quote Agent all sell AI quoting to exactly this buyer. Closed.
6. FAI / AS9102 report generation for small shops. Dropped at screen — High QA, 1factory, InspectionXpert, DISCUS, GroundControl and CADNexa all occupy it; nothing left for a narrow wedge.
7. Cold-email reputation guardian for AI-SDR users (from the Explee bookmark). Dropped at screen — Instantly, Warmy, Mailforge, Warmforge and Alta all sell deliverability monitoring and domain warming; commodity, and the buyer is a churn-prone solo founder.
8. Cognitive-debt reviewer: flags PRs a human cannot explain, from the Addy Osmani article. Dropped at generation — latent pain, no budget holder, and another developer-tools entry.
9. Plaid-for-benefits wedge: document-reuse layer for a single county benefits office (YC RFS, Gustaf Alströmer). Dropped at screen — a strong signal but a 12-18 month government sales cycle, far outside an evenings-and-weekends builder's reach to first revenue.
10. AI-for-City-Hall wedge: plan-review corrections for small building departments (YC RFS). Dropped — Archistar AI PreCheck already sells city-side AI code and zoning review to 30+ local governments, and the filed idea Backcheck already serves the applicant side of the same correction-letter workflow. Repeat plus a closed gap.
11. Vendor-cert verification for medical-device contract manufacturers. Folded into the pick as an expansion market rather than run as a separate candidate — same workflow, different regulatory vocabulary.

PROJECT
1. Strangers — drop a lockfile, see how many distinct humans can execute code on your machine, plus who published while you slept → PICK. Personal number, instantly postable, weekly reason to return, every data field verified free and unauthenticated. 2. Cooldown Check — paste a lockfile, see which installed versions are younger than 7 days → finalist, folded into Strangers as one panel; alone it's a yes/no answer nobody screenshots. 3. Provenance Scorecard — what share of your deps are published via trusted publishing → finalist, also folded in; too abstract to lead with. 4. HackerTube Shelf — the 6,454 HN videos as a browsable shelf → dropped at screen, repeat of Canon (2026-11-01). 5. Teardown Gallery — a public gallery of Elvar's teardown-skill 3D machine sims → dropped, it's hosting someone else's project, not a tool. 6. Startup Follower Racer — weekly leaderboard of fastest-growing startup X accounts → dropped at screen, needs paid X API and benln's screenshot is already the product. 7. Agent Surrender Score — grade a chat transcript on how much you deferred to the agent (from Osmani) → dropped, judgment is subjective and unfalsifiable, output is a scolding nobody posts. 8. Secrets Sweep — paste a repo URL, find exposed .env keys → dropped at screen, gitleaks/trufflehog own this and scanning other people's repos is sketchy. 9. SIP Friction Meter — visualise how many steps Indian MF onboarding takes → dropped, no data source, narrow audience, and it's marketing for someone else's app. 10. CNC Quote Decoder — upload a CAD part, get a machinability score → dropped, overlaps tonight's venture (machine shops) and needs real geometry processing, far past a weekend.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): summarised twentyfour26 and the state of on-demand CNC bottlenecks (surfaced quoting, setup, outside processes and cert/inspection as the real constraints — this is where the pick came from); summarised Explee (pay-as-you-go AI SDR at ~$0.04/email, crowded field — killed candidate 7 early); summarised the Jack Cable security guide (npm cooldown / minimum release age advice — seeded candidate 4) and the Addy Osmani cognitive-debt article. Screening pot (6 of 6): one search each on CNC quoting software (Paperless Parts, Uptool, AMFG — closed), dependency-cooldown tooling (Safeguard.sh — closed), Indian MFD back-office software (Mindstack, Creso, REDVision — closed and a repeat of Shortfall), outside-process vendor tracking (thin results, the promising signal), cold-email deliverability (Instantly, Warmy — closed), FAI/AS9102 software (High QA, 1factory, GroundControl — closed). Deep research pot (12 of 12): ERP handling of outside processing and user complaints; dedicated outside-processing/subcontract products and ERP pricing; AI voice agents chasing supplier dates (HappyRobot/Conversight/VoiceRun) and whether they serve SMBs; AI-for-City-Hall landscape (Archistar) which killed candidate 10; GroundControl's PO Review category, funding and pricing model; AS9100 8.4.3 flowdown obligations and failure consequences; cert-package assembly effort and the $250-per-shipment penalty example; RFQ/quoting economics for sub-20-person shops; US machine-shop establishment counts and expediter roles; CoC-vs-PO automated checking (LandingAI, Certivo); what actually goes in an outside-process PO packet and how revision errors happen. Deep research reshaped the idea twice: it closed quoting and FAI, and it pushed the wedge from date-chasing to the document loop. Sharpening pot (5 of 5): confirmed SMB software price bands (Uptool $195-495, 1factory $75/user/mo, ProShop ~$500-715) for market_pull; confirmed aerospace/defense backlog growth (PwC, Oliver Wyman) for timing; confirmed no ERP does the chase-and-file loop natively (only third-party bolt-ons) for gap; checked go-to-market channels for small shops (founder-led, trade media, referrals — tempered the wedge score); checked whether an email-in procurement agent already exists as a product (FactoryJet is a custom-build agency, not a packaged product — leaves the gap open). Investor signals weighed: a16z "Startups tame the chaos of multimodal data" (Jennifer Li) and "AI reinforces business models" / "Forward-deployed motions take AI to the 99%" supported the pick; YC's "The $15-an-Hour Expert" and "AI for City Hall" were both tested — the first reinforced the pick's framing, the second was dropped after Archistar and the filed Backcheck idea closed it. YC's space, robots-in-America and data-center-supply-chain signals were set aside as capital-intensive and far outside this builder's reach.
Sharpening (7 to 7.8): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6.5). The first shape was a generic "outside-processing tracker: see what's out and chase the date." Research showed that half is crowded from both ends: every job-shop ERP already records an outside-process PO, and HappyRobot, Conversight and VoiceRun all now sell supplier delivery-date chasing agents. Change to the idea: moved the centre of gravity from date-chasing to the regulated document loop — flow the customer's invoked spec revision and quality clauses into the processor PO, then verify the returned cert against exactly those requirements, with date-chasing as the supporting feature. Evidence that the reshaped version holds: Perplexity on AS9100 8.4.3 confirmed flowdown to special-process suppliers is mandatory and that wrong-revision or missing-cert failures produce SCARs, shipment rejection and audit findings; a Perplexity sweep of ERPs found no native "email the processor and auto-file the cert against the requirement" loop in ProShop, JobBOSS² or Fulcrum, and the only such capability found was third-party bolt-on automations — i.e. people are building it by hand; LandingAI does PO-vs-CoC checking but sells to electronics enterprises, not job shops. gap 6.5→8, pain 7→8.

Round 2 — weakest criterion: market_pull (6.5). Worry: can a 25-person shop pay for another tool, and who signs? Change to the idea: narrowed the buyer from "any machine shop" to AS9100/defense-exposed shops of 10-80 people where the owner or quality manager signs, and set the price inside an existing budget band rather than inventing one. Evidence: Uptool publishes $195/month with most shops at $195-495; 1factory lists $75/user/month with a 5-user minimum including CoC and SCAR workflows; ProShop is estimated ~$500-715/month for small shops — so $300-600 is a familiar number. PwC's near-15,000-unit commercial backlog and >50% three-year defense backlog growth, plus Oliver Wyman's finding that 45% of suppliers cannot double output within a year, support rising regulated work at exactly these shops. What did NOT survive: I looked for a quantified "days lost at outside processors" or job-shop on-time-delivery benchmark and found none, and no public evidence that shops buy a standalone line item for this specific workflow. So market_pull moved only 6.5→7.5, not higher, and the validation test was written to attack precisely that hole. timing 7.5→8 on the 2026 supplier-chasing agent category plus the a16z multimodal-data signal. wedge held at 7.5: v1 is email-in, no ERP integration, sellable in weeks, but it is a regulated-document product so trust-building slows the first close.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Karpathy HackerTube dataset (confirmed the zip is 6,454 videos + 39,834 labelled comments + a 150-topic taxonomy — but Canon already in the library covers that angle, so I dropped it); the Jack Cable security guide behind the Scott Wu bookmark (the 7-day minimum release age, lockfile and credential advice became the spine of tonight's pick); and the Addy Osmani article (critical thinking when agents do the work — interesting but produced only essay-shaped candidates). Screening pot (5/5): checked cooldown tooling (cooldowns.dev is a config reference, not a scanner), lockfile paste-in prior art (Socket is CI/SaaS, npmgraph draws graphs not people), startup-follower-growth trackers (crowded, and the data needs paid X API), and "too new dependency" checkers (all CLI/CI, no web). Deep pot (8/8): verified registry.npmjs.org packument fields (maintainers, _npmUser, time, dist.attestations, hasInstallScript in lockfiles), CORS and anonymous rate-limit reality, the downloads API, and the closest prior art — rsscan --deps, which proves the counting works (433 packages → 275 publishers) but is a CLI with no visual, no card and no watch. Sharpen pot (4/4, counted within deep/sharpen split): confirmed Dependabot's weekly digest is security-alerts-only, confirmed trusted-publishing adoption is a live 2026 story, confirmed no free web tool produces an aggregate trust-footprint number. Net change: the idea moved from "pretty dependency visual" to "one personal number + weekly delta + copy-paste fix", and buildability was capped at 8 because of the unproven 1,000-fetch rate-limit question.
Sharpening (7.4 to 8): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (6 before). The v1 was a one-time number: scan, screenshot, done. Change to the idea: a "Watch this lockfile" mode that stores the tree fingerprint locally and, when you come back (or after a weekly nudge), shows the delta — which of your dependencies published a new version, which gained or changed maintainers, which are still inside the 7-day cooldown window. Research: npm packuments carry per-version publish timestamps in the `time` map and per-version `_npmUser`, so the delta is computable client-side with no backend (https://github.com/npm/registry/blob/main/docs/REGISTRY-API.md); and I checked the obvious incumbent — Dependabot's weekly digest covers security alerts only, not "who published into your tree this week", and nothing found does maintainer-change tracking for individuals (https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/dependabot-alerts). Usefulness 6 → 8. Round 2 — weak criterion: freshness (7 before). Added the provenance/trusted-publishing dimension: show what share of your tree is published through OIDC trusted publishing with an attestation versus a long-lived token. Research confirmed `dist.attestations` is exposed in packuments and trusted publishing only reached meaningful adoption in 2026, with roughly half of npm's top packages still not using it (https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements/, https://getcommit.dev/blog/). That makes the headline genuinely not-computable-cleanly a year ago. Freshness 7 → 8. Buildability held at 8 rather than 9: registry CORS is documented as supported but historically inconsistent on error responses (https://github.com/npm/feedback/discussions/117) and anonymous 429s are real, so a tiny proxy may be needed — checked, but not proven at 1,000-package scale.
prototype_summary: A clickable Outbound control-tower prototype for Keystone Precision Machining showing 11 outside-processing lots, a whiteboard-vs-Outbound toggle, an agent chase-email that updates a late promise date, clause flowdown onto a processor PO, a cert that fails spec-revision and lot-traceability checks, and per-PO ship-readiness cards.
